data.pattern_summary: Kadane's Algorithm maintains a running sum of the current subarray, resetting it when it drops below zero, which allows finding the maximum subarray sum in linear time.

pattern_options.name: Kadane's Algorithm
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. This pattern tracks the maximum sum ending at each position by deciding whether to extend the previous subarray or start a fresh one.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers usually work when elements are strictly positive or when moving a pointer has a monotonic effect on the sum, which negative numbers break here.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows require a fixed size or a condition where expanding and shrinking the window predictably grows or shrinks the metric, which fails with negative numbers.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. The array is not sorted, and the property of subarray sums is not monotonic, so binary search does not apply.

signals.hint: Implies the elements must be next to each other in the original array, ruling out sorting or picking random elements.
Indicates an optimization problem where we want to find the highest accumulated value.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach uses two nested loops to check every possible starting and ending index for a subarray, calculates the sum for each slice, and keeps track of the largest sum found.
data.brute_force_why: There are O(n^2) possible subarrays, and for each one, the built-in sum() operation takes up to O(n) time, resulting in cubic time complexity.
data.bottleneck: Line 5 repeatedly computes the sum of overlapping slices from scratch, doing redundant work instead of reusing the sum computed in the previous step.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times the same elements are added together across different subarrays.
If you know the sum of a subarray up to index j, do you need to re-add everything to find the sum up to j+1?
Think about how the previous subarray sum can help you calculate the current subarray sum in constant time.

data.overview: Kadane's algorithm finds the contiguous subarray with the largest sum by iterating through the array and tracking the maximum sum ending at the current position. At each step, it decides whether to extend the previous subarray or start fresh from the current element.
data.intuition: Imagine walking down a path collecting coins or paying tolls represented by numbers. If the total coins in your pocket drop below zero, you are better off dropping your past collection and starting fresh from the current spot.

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly recalculates subarray sums, leading to redundant work. Kadane's algorithm removes this bottleneck by making a single pass through the array, dynamically deciding at each step whether to extend the previous subarray or start a new one.

derivation.note: The loop iterates through the remaining elements of the array.
Performs constant time comparison and addition.

data.time_summary: Lines 4, 5, and 6 run proportionally to n. Summing these costs yields O(n) total time, which matches the measured evidence showing steps scaling linearly with input size.
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar variables are used to track the current and global maximums, requiring O(1) auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When finding optimal contiguous subarrays, try tracking a running state that decides whether to discard past elements at each step.
mistakes: Failing to initialize maximum trackers with the first element of the array instead of zero, which breaks when all elements are negative.
Resetting the current sum to zero instead of the current element when a negative prefix drops the sum below the element itself.
